hook.line: Vale is writing the café's first newsletter, and every line has a reason behind it: so the neighbours come back, so they try the new bread. When the reason is about someone else doing something, Spanish adds one small word.
hook.es: Vale hace pan de queso para que los clientes vuelvan.
hook.en: Vale makes cheese bread so that the customers come back.

examples.es: Te dejo la llave para que abras mañana.
examples.en: I'm leaving you the key so you can open tomorrow. (to a friend)

examples.es: Hablo despacio para que me entiendas.
examples.en: I speak slowly so that you understand me. (to a friend)

examples.es: Mariana nos mandó el artículo para que lo leamos.
examples.en: Mariana sent us the article so that we'd read it.

examples.es: Te llamo para que no te preocupes.
examples.en: I'm calling so you won't worry. (to a friend)

examples.es: ¿Qué hago para que Simón no hable tanto?
examples.en: What do I do so that Simón doesn't talk so much?

examples.es: Abrimos temprano para que los taxistas tomen un tinto.
examples.en: We open early so the taxi drivers can have a black coffee.

examples.es: Guardé un pedazo de torta para que lo pruebes.
examples.en: I saved a piece of cake so you can try it. (to a friend)

rule:
You already say why you do things with *para* plus the plain verb: *Ahorro plata para comprar un carro.* I save, I buy.

When the second action belongs to someone else, Spanish says *para que* and uses the wish form, the same one you know from *quiero que*:
*Te dejo la llave para que abras.* I leave the key, you open.
*Hablo despacio para que me entiendas.* I speak, you understand.

English hides this in many ways: so you can, so that you'll, for you to. Spanish has one: *para que* plus the wish form. You don't need *puedas* or a future, just *abras*, *entiendas*, *vuelvan*.

Two things never happen after *para que*: the plain verb (*para que abrir*) and the ordinary present (*para que abres*).
smallPrint: Teachers call this a purpose clause (*oración final*). *Para que* always takes the present subjunctive.

options: I'm leaving you the key so you can open tomorrow. (to a friend)
I'm leaving you the key so I can open tomorrow.
I need your number so you can call me. (to a friend)
I need your number to call you. (to a friend)

options: I'm giving you my number so I can call you. (to a friend)

options: Mariana sent us the article so she could read it.

options: What do I do so that I don't talk so much?

What do I do so that Simón doesn't talk so much?

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *abres* or *abras* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Te dejo la llave para que ___ mañana.*
yourTurn.answer: Te dejo la llave para que abras mañana.
yourTurn.why: After *para que*, always the wish form: *abras*.

yourTurn.prompt: Pick *llamarme* or *que me llames* and type the whole sentence, to a friend: *Te doy mi número para ___.* (so you can call me)
yourTurn.answer: Te doy mi número para que me llames.
yourTurn.why: Your friend does the calling, so *para que me llames*.

yourTurn.prompt: Tell a friend: I'm calling so you won't worry.
yourTurn.answer: Te llamo para que no te preocupes.
yourTurn.why: Your friend does the worrying, so *para que* and *preocupes*.

yourTurn.prompt: Type in Spanish: We open early so the taxi drivers can have a black coffee.
yourTurn.answer: Abrimos temprano para que los taxistas tomen un tinto.
yourTurn.why: The drivers do the drinking, so *para que tomen*. No *puedan* needed.

yourTurn.prompt: Tell a friend: I saved a piece of cake so you can try it.
yourTurn.answer: Guardé un pedazo de torta para que lo pruebes.
accept: Te guardé un pedazo de torta para que lo pruebes.
yourTurn.why: *Probar* becomes *pruebes* for *tú*, and *lo* is the piece.

yourTurn.prompt: Change who does it. Now you're saving so your son can buy a car: *Ahorro plata para comprar un carro.*
yourTurn.answer: Ahorro plata para que mi hijo compre un carro.
yourTurn.why: A second person buys, so *para que* and the wish form *compre*.

yourTurn.prompt: Say it to you all (*ustedes*): *Te llamo para que no te preocupes.*
yourTurn.answer: Los llamo para que no se preocupen.
yourTurn.why: For *ustedes*, *te* becomes *los* and *se*, and the verb ends in *n*.

pitfalls.wrong: Te dejo la llave para que abres mañana.
pitfalls.right: Te dejo la llave para que abras mañana.
pitfalls.why: Almost. *Para que* always takes the wish form: *abras*, not *abres*.

pitfalls.wrong: Te doy mi número para llamarme.
pitfalls.right: Te doy mi número para que me llames.
pitfalls.why: With the plain verb, the caller is you. Your friend calls, so *para que me llames*.

pitfalls.wrong: Ahorro plata para que compre un carro.
pitfalls.right: Ahorro plata para comprar un carro.
pitfalls.why: If you're the one buying, drop *que* and use the plain verb.

personal: Write two true lines about something you do for someone else, and why: *Llamo a mi mamá los domingos para que...*, *Cocino los sábados para que...*
